title: Robot Pilot Guild for Gaming-Native Gen Z
one_liner: A guild that recruits, trains and certifies gamers aged 16-25 to remotely pilot delivery robots and humanoids, with a portable verified flight-hour logbook that becomes their credential.
customer: Robotics and physical-AI companies (sidewalk delivery, warehouse, humanoid pilots) that buy validated pilot-hours and demonstration data. Workforce boards and trainees pay for certification.
problem: Robots in 2026 run on human backup: remote assistance for stuck delivery robots and teleoperated demonstrations to train humanoids. Companies staff this ad hoc through BPOs and labeling vendors, with high churn, uneven quality and no career ladder. US lab teleoperator roles are already posting at $30-$55 per hour. Gen Alpha and Gen Z raised on controllers have the reflexes but no legitimate on-ramp.
solution: Regional 'pilot houses' with standardized rigs plus at-home certification. A tiered license runs from Level 1 sidewalk assist to Level 3 dexterous manipulation, tested in simulation and on real robots. The guild is the W-2 employer of record, sells SLA-bound pilot capacity by the validated hour, and records verified hours in a portable logbook like aviation. Quality is managed through replay review and per-task acceptance rates.
why_now: Teleoperation sits at the center of humanoid and home-robot programs in 2026 (home humanoids such as 1X NEO ship with remote operators), and demonstration data is being bought like compute. Entry-level white-collar hiring is weak, so young people want alternative on-ramps. Robot companies need reliable operator supply now, not in 2030.
revenue_model: $25-$45 per validated pilot-hour billed to robot companies, targeting about 40% gross margin. Certification fees of $200-$600 paid by trainees, workforce funds or employers, plus placement fees when companies hire pilots directly.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset in physical AI is consistent, high-quality human motor demonstration, and Gen Alpha has been practicing exactly that skill for a decade. A verified flight-hour logbook turns play into a portable credential. That makes workers stickier and quality auditable, so this is a licensed guild employer rather than a gig marketplace.
first_30_days: Approach three sidewalk-delivery or warehouse-robot startups with visible remote-assist queues. Offer a paid 4-week pilot with 10 trained gamers recruited from Discord communities and community-college esports programs. Train them on the customer's own simulator and bill per validated hour. Goal: one signed pilot and one letter of intent for a 50-pilot cohort.

title: 72-Hour Diligence Engine for Vet Clinic Acquirers
one_liner: Upload a PIMS export and P&L and get retention cohorts, price-versus-volume decomposition and doctor-dependence risk in three days, then keep the same schema as the post-close KPI dashboard.
customer: Mid-size vet groups, search-fund and PE platforms buying 5-50 clinics a year, and practice lenders.
problem: Roll-ups are continuing (GoodVets buying WellHaven, 40+ hospitals), but small acquirers rely on broker packages and QuickBooks. PIMS exports differ by system, and price increases can hide falling active-client counts, a real risk given visits reportedly down three years.
solution: Ingest PIMS exports across major systems, normalize service lines, then compute cohort retention, active clients, revenue per DVM and tech utilization, price/mix/volume decomposition, discount and controlled-substance anomalies, and revenue at risk if the owner-vet leaves. Output a quality-of-earnings-lite memo, then continue as a post-merger KPI dashboard.
why_now: M&A pace is high, buyers include newer and smaller platforms without in-house analytics, and LLMs make messy export mapping cheap. Incumbents such as IDEXX are buying workflow AI (CoVet), not diligence tooling.
revenue_model: $3-6K per target for diligence, $1-2K per clinic per month for post-close dashboards.
non_obvious_insight: The price hikes that flatter EBITDA may be masking client attrition. Diligence that sees through price versus volume is worth far more than its fee, and brokers will not build it because it works against their headline numbers.
first_30_days: Approach 10 mid-size groups and search funds with a free retrospective on one closed deal. Build export mappers for 3 major PIMS. Sell 3 paid diligences at $3K each.

title: Cool-Hours Slot Exchange for Tour Operators
angle: Pairing 1: Climate adaptation x Travel/hospitality (overtourism and extreme heat)
one_liner: Forecast-driven heat re-scheduling for tour operators, plus a marketplace that sells 7am and 8pm venue slots, turning the coolest hours of the day into a priced, allocated resource.
customer: Independent ground-tour operators, destination management companies and cruise shore-excursion desks (10-200 guides) in Athens, Rome, Seville, Marrakech, Petra and Kyoto. The supply side is private venues (wineries, palazzi, small museums, cooking schools) with unused early and late capacity.
problem: Overtourism policy fixates on fees and caps, but the real crush is temporal: coaches, lunch and check-out times funnel everyone into 10:00-15:00, exactly when heat peaks. Operators cancel and refund ad hoc, guides carry heat-illness risk, and there is no record of duty-of-care decisions for insurers under package-travel liability. Meanwhile venues sit empty at dawn and dusk.
solution: Three layers. (1) A scheduler that ingests 5-day heat-stress (WBGT/UTCI) forecasts and the operator's tour book, rebuilds itineraries (dawn starts, indoor midday, evening loops), messages guests in their language and re-checks availability. (2) A time-stamped duty-of-care log (decisions, water and shade stops, guest health flags) exportable to insurers. (3) A slot exchange where venues list early and late timed entries at a premium and operators buy allotments in bulk. Venues get demand data to justify extended hours.
why_now: Summer 2026 Europe saw record heat and a reported provisional death toll near 38,000 (secondary source), pushing operators and regulators toward heat rules. Destinations are moving from fees to allocation: Venice's day-tripper fee reportedly did not cut numbers, while Mount Fuji's hard 4,000/day cap plus fee works. Allocation needs tooling nobody has built. Margins are squeezed by jet-fuel-driven cost increases, so avoiding refunds matters.
revenue_model: EUR 199-499 per month SaaS per operator (tiered by guide count), 4-6% take on slot-exchange GMV, and paid analytics for venues and DMOs ($10-30K per year).
non_obvious_insight: Heat converts overtourism from a space problem into a time problem, and cool hours are the unpriced scarce commodity. They can be allocated like airport slots. Operators are natural demand aggregators, so a small team can win venue supply by promising bulk purchase. The duty-of-care log is what gets insurers interested, because it cuts claim exposure.
first_30_days: Interview 20 Athens and Rome operators about summer 2026 heat-day losses. Build the scheduler as a WhatsApp plus Google Sheets workflow on open forecast data for 5 pilot operators. Get 5 private venues to commit to 08:00 or 19:30 allotments. Demo at WTM London (Nov 2026) and FITUR Madrid (Jan 2027), and convert pilots to paid before the 2027 season.

title: Groundskeepers: Custodianship for AI-Built Software
one_liner: Property management for software: a monthly subscription where a named junior-developer 'groundskeeper' keeps small businesses' AI-built apps patched, backed up, monitored, and alive, with a senior signing off.
customer: SMBs (multi-location dentists, HVAC firms, property managers, boutique agencies) and solo founders who built internal tools or products with Lovable, Replit, Cursor and similar. $149-499/month per app. Agencies that built apps for clients can white-label.
problem: Building is free but owning is not. 'Vibe-code cleanup' is a recognized freelance niche, but it is a one-time project. After the rescue no one is responsible for dependency updates, key rotation, backups, uptime, model deprecations, and API changes, and a large share of production vibe-coded apps hit an incident within 90 days.
solution: A fixed-price move-in inspection ($900), then a monthly custody plan with monitoring, patching, backup verification, a lightweight quarterly security check, a runbook, and one accountable human with an incident SLA. Groundskeepers are laid-off junior developers, each managing 25-40 apps on a standardized template stack with AI tooling, supervised by fractional seniors. The plan includes an 'exit ramp' to rebuild or retire the app.
why_now: In 2026 a flood of AI-built apps entered production and cleanup specialists are one of the fastest-growing freelance niches, per Forbes coverage. Junior developer hiring has dried up, so skilled, cheap talent is abundant. Cyber insurers are beginning to care about managed versus unmanaged apps.
revenue_model: Recurring subscription, inspection fees, incident retainers, exit-ramp rebuilds, and referral fees from cyber insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The market frames this as cleanup (a project) but the durable business is custody (a relationship), like property management versus house flipping. The same structure gives displaced juniors a career ladder: custody is the residency that produces the senior engineers the industry stopped training.
first_30_days: Offer free move-in inspections to the first 20 apps through Lovable and Replit communities, local chambers of commerce, and SMB Facebook groups. Hire 2 laid-off juniors. Assemble monitoring from off-the-shelf tools (Sentry, uptime checks, Dependabot). Target 15 paying customers at about $199, roughly $3k monthly recurring revenue, by day 90.

title: Valet Keys for Delegated Browser Sessions
one_liner: An enforcement layer that lets an agent act inside your logged-in bank, airline or supplier portal, but only within per-site limits such as read-only here and a spend cap there.
customer: Enterprise finance-ops, revenue-cycle and logistics teams running browser agents on portals with no API (20-500 seats), followed by builders of prosumer browser agents who need a safety story.
problem: Insiders are building agent identity (OAuth for agents), but most delegated work rides on cookies in sites with no API. The agent inherits the user's full session. Browsers offer no primitive for a user to see, scope or withdraw an agent's access. If the user is legally the one who accessed the site, as the Ninth Circuit reasoned, the user owns everything the agent does with that session.
solution: A browser extension plus enforcement proxy with per-site policy packs that classify actions (view, draft, submit, pay, change credentials) using URL, DOM and network patterns. Irreversible actions are denied by default, with spend and count caps, step-up approval and signed action receipts. Ship maintained packs for the top 200 enterprise portals (payer, carrier, marketplace seller-center and bank portals) and update them as sites change.
why_now: Browser agents went mainstream in 2026, and about 21,600 OpenClaw instances were found exposed. Machine identities outnumber humans roughly 109 to 1, and the agent-equals-user doctrine puts liability on the delegating user.
revenue_model: $15-40 per seat per month for enterprises, policy-pack subscriptions, and a per-session API price for agent vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The missing primitive is a valet key (parks the car, cannot open the trunk) for sessions. The moat is the maintained per-site action taxonomy, which is tedious, unglamorous and hard to copy.
first_30_days: Find one revenue-cycle or logistics ops team already using browser agents and build read-only plus draft-only policy packs for the 5 portals they use. Run a $2k/month pilot and log blocked actions as proof of value.

title: Costly-Commitment Kits for Fitness Congregations
one_liner: A retention product for boutique gyms and run clubs that borrows religion's real community mechanism, costly commitment, to turn members into a congregation.
customer: Owners of boutique fitness studios, CrossFit boxes, climbing gyms and multi-site run clubs, with franchisors as the scale channel.
problem: Gen Z made up 47% of new gym joins in 2025 yet posts the highest churn (around 54% in one industry dataset), and nearly half of them say community is why they stay. Studios respond with discounts, apps and easier joining, which attracts free-riders and does not build attachment.
solution: A kit of printed rites, a coach's liturgy guide and light software: an initiation for a founding cohort, attendance vows made to a partner, earned 'colors' for milestones, a dawn 'vigil' class, rites for return-from-injury and for a member's death, and a warm leaving ritual. We A/B the kit across studios against controls on 90-day retention.
why_now: ABC Fitness's 2025 year-end report shows Gen Z dominating new joins and community as a top reason to stay. Run clubs and studios are already positioned as a substitute for church, and retention is the KPI that owners pay to move.
revenue_model: $199-499 per month per studio for the kit and software, a performance option of about 10% of measured retention gains, and licensing to franchisors across their locations.
non_obvious_insight: The whole industry builds community by removing friction, while religious sociology (Iannaccone's 'Why Strict Churches Are Strong') finds that commitment, sacrifice and visible costs create strong communities and free-rider filters. Add cost that feels like meaning (time, visibility, obligation) instead of a fee and members become attached, so the friction studios fear is the mechanism.
first_30_days: Recruit five studios from one local franchise. Run a founding-cohort covenant for new joiners and compare 90-day retention against control cohorts. Publish the result and pitch it to franchise developers.

title: Spray-Drone Service Depots for Grounded Fleets
one_liner: Independent repair, parts and loaner service for the roughly 80% of US spray drones that are DJI Agras.
customer: Custom aerial applicators, ag retailers and farm co-ops running spray-drone fleets.
problem: DJI was added to the FCC Covered List in December 2025, new T55 and T100 models have no committed US launch, and applicators face limited drones and parts.
solution: A depot network with a parts pool, battery service, pump and arm repair, calibration and a loaner fleet, plus operator training and compliance support.
why_now: The ban freezes new models while the installed base must keep flying for years, and everyone else is chasing US-made OEM hardware.
revenue_model: Repair fees, parts margin and annual maintenance contracts per drone.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody builds a service moat because the attention goes to replacement hardware. The installed base is the durable revenue pool and needs only lawful repair and parts.
first_30_days: Buy a starter parts inventory, set up a depot in one spray-heavy region such as the Texas or Arkansas Delta, and sign 10 applicators to maintenance contracts.

title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. Sign 5-10 brands on a paid pilot, record their marks, and produce the first product-identification guides. Line up one IP law firm as the enforcement referral partner.

title: Data Act Unlock for Hotel Connected Equipment
one_liner: Use the EU Data Act's user-access rights to pull hotels' own data out of locked vendor clouds (HVAC, locks, laundry, elevators) into an energy and maintenance ledger that third-party service firms can plug into.
customer: EU independent hotel groups and management companies with 5-50 properties, plus independent HVAC, elevator and kitchen-equipment service firms and energy-optimization vendors that want the data.
problem: After the 2026 Hormuz energy shock, hotel energy costs have been repriced sharply. The data from a hotel's connected thermostats, HVAC, locks, laundry and elevators is trapped in manufacturers' clouds, resold as premium dashboards or API fees. A mixed-brand group cannot build a unified view, and independent maintenance firms cannot diagnose without OEM tools.
solution: Since Sep 2025 the Data Act has let users demand the data generated by connected products and have it shared with a third party they choose (free to the user, on my reading, so verify). New products must offer access by design from 12 Sep 2026. The service is a request desk (letter templates, deadline tracking per OEM, escalation to the national authority) plus connectors that load the data into a property energy and asset ledger, with consent logs for designated recipients.
why_now: The Sep 2026 design-by-default date has just passed and vendors are unprepared, so early requests set the precedents. Energy-cost pain makes the hotel side motivated. The brief also shows small hardware makers scrambling with Data Act and CRA duties, so vendors are stretched.
revenue_model: About EUR 200 per property per month, 10-15% of verified energy savings, and onboarding fees paid by service firms and optimizers who become designated recipients.
non_obvious_insight: Hotels are among the largest accidental 'users' under the Data Act, with dozens of connected products per building, and nobody has told them. The law turns vendor lock-in into a right, the way GDPR created a market for data-subject-request services.
first_30_days: Sign one 10-property group for a flat EUR 1,500 'Data Act audit plus first requests'. Inventory its connected assets, send about 20 access requests across 5 OEMs, and document responses and escalations. Then sell the same audit to 4 more groups and pitch one independent service firm as a designated recipient.

title: Post-Mortem CT Plus Remote Pathology for Coroners
one_liner: Give rural coroners a scan-and-remote-read pathway so cause-of-death answers arrive in a day instead of weeks, without buying a single scanner.
customer: County coroners and medical examiners in rural or under-resourced jurisdictions, state ME systems, and hospitals with after-hours CT capacity.
problem: There is a well-documented shortage of forensic pathologists. Many rural coroners are elected non-physicians, autopsies are outsourced hundreds of miles away with multi-week backlogs, and each autopsy costs thousands. Families can't finalize burial or estates without a death certificate.
solution: A protocol in which the body is scanned on a hospital CT off-hours (or a mobile unit), with external-exam photos uploaded to a network of board-certified forensic pathologists and radiologists. AI triage flags fractures, hemorrhage and foreign objects, and the coroner gets a 24-hour read with a recommendation on whether a full autopsy is needed. The coroner keeps statutory authority.
why_now: Post-mortem CT is routine in several countries, imaging AI has matured, and telepathology infrastructure exists. The forensic pathology shortage persists, and overdose and heat deaths have strained offices.
revenue_model: $600-$1,200 per case plus $30-$60K/year county retainers, with rental fees to hospitals for scanner time.
non_obvious_insight: The slowest step in death care isn't the funeral, it's the death certificate, and each day of delay costs families and insurers. A software-plus-network layer can loosen the choke point without owning capital equipment.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 forensic pathologists (retired or part-time) as remote readers. Approach 5 backlogged rural coroners and one rural hospital about a pilot. Expect pilot signing within 6 months, with full revenue closer to 12.

title: Supplier-Funded Books for Trade-Credit Customers
one_liner: Regional distributors pay to give each micro-customer done-for-you books, and get a permissioned live view of that customer's credit risk.
customer: Regional wholesale distributors (foodservice, produce, beauty supply, auto parts, building materials, uniform and linen) with 500-10,000 micro accounts on net-30 terms.
problem: Distributors extend trade credit to taquerias, salons and garages on gut feel, and bad debt and slow pay eat margin. Micro-customers keep no books, so there is no data to underwrite against. Ramp and Brex have moved upmarket and no vendor serves this tier. The owners will not pay for bookkeeping themselves.
solution: Every active account gets free, done-for-you books, funded by the distributor. Bank and card feeds are connected, the distributor's own invoices are auto-ingested, and receipts arrive by text or WhatsApp. The customer owns the ledger and can export it any time. With the customer's opt-in, the distributor sees cash coverage, the aging of the customer's other bills and payment-risk flags, and can raise limits or offer early-pay discounts to accounts that look healthy.
why_now: LLM categorization pushes cost per account below about $10 a month. The Fed's 2026 data shows microfirms are cash-tight (22% of applicants got no financing, and nonemployers lean on personal funds). The Bench collapse made data ownership and portability a selling point.
revenue_model: The distributor pays $10-25 per active account per month, justified by bad-debt reduction, shorter DSO and lower churn. Upsells: tax filing, payroll, and early-payment financing with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The micro-business will never pay for bookkeeping, but the party carrying its receivable will. A bad account costs a distributor thousands, while $15 a month is noise. Sponsorship also raises switching costs, so the distributor gets retention for free.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical in one metro, such as a produce or beauty-supply distributor. Get 12 months of invoices and payment history for 100 accounts, then backtest whether simple books-derived signals predict late payment. Sign a paid pilot covering 100 accounts, with success defined as DSO and write-offs.

title: Screwworm-Era Rescue Transport Compliance Desk
one_liner: With screwworm confirmed in Texas, dogs leaving Texas and New Mexico need a fresh vet inspection certificate and destination permits; run the compliance desk that keeps shelter transports moving.
customer: Texas and New Mexico shelters, rescue transport organizations (ground and air), destination shelters in other states, and the funders who pay for transport.
problem: New World screwworm was first confirmed in Texas on 2026-06-03, with movement restrictions in infested zones across a growing list of counties. Reports say dogs from Texas and New Mexico now need a certificate of veterinary inspection within 72 hours of movement that attests no wounds infested with screwworm. Receiving states add entry permits and pre-travel inspections five to seven days out, shelter transports are slowing, and accredited vets are scarce for 20-100 animal loads.
solution: A transport desk with a destination-state rules engine, permit and eCVI orchestration, scheduling of mobile inspection crews (floating DVM plus techs) at pickup sites, a treatment log for authorized products, manifests, and rejection-risk alerts before a truck leaves.
why_now: Screwworm's first US detection (June 2026), FDA emergency authorizations for animal drugs (15 EUAs and 3 conditional approvals as of 2026-09-03), and state zone orders have changed movement rules mid-season. Shelters are crowded and funders are looking for what unblocks flow.
revenue_model: $15-35 per animal moved, mobile inspection crew fees, and SaaS for destination shelters. Costs often covered by transport grants.
non_obvious_insight: Rescue transport is treated as a charity logistics problem. The new binding constraints are regulatory paperwork and scarce accredited-vet hours, which is a compliance-ops business with per-animal pricing. The same rails will be reused for the next outbreak (H5N1, canine influenza, rabies rule changes).
first_30_days: Call 10 Texas shelters and transport groups. Put the top 5 destination-state rule sets into a spreadsheet. Run 2 transports with hired mobile-vet pickup inspections at $20 per animal. Approach transport-grant funders for direct payment.

title: Finishing Milk Run for Small Machine Shops
one_liner: A scheduled truck route and capacity-slot exchange that pools small lots from many shops into full tank loads and racks at platers, anodizers, heat treaters and powder coaters.
customer: Job shops and small OEM plants (5-150 employees) that machine or fabricate parts but outsource plating, anodize, passivation, heat treat, e-coat or powder coat. The buyer is the shop owner or plant manager. The second customer is the finisher, who gets fuller tanks and lines.
problem: Everyone talks about a shortage of machinists, but the real reshoring bottleneck is finishing. Parts wait 9-15 days for a truck and for enough volume to fill a tank or rack. Finishers apply minimum-charge lots that punish small runs. Shops drive parts themselves or pay LTL rates of $150-$300 per pallet, and a batch's lead time is mostly waiting, not processing. The 2026 Reshoring Initiative data show finishing capacity as part of the bottleneck, and permits make new capacity slow and rare.
solution: Run daily box-truck routes around a dense corridor (Akron-Canton-Cleveland-Youngstown) with QR-coded totes and text-message status. Pre-buy weekly capacity slots at 8-12 vetted finishers, pool many shops' small lots into shared racks, and guarantee 3-5 day door-to-door turnaround. Route data and slot utilisation decide which finisher gets which parts. Expand to a second corridor (Columbus-Dayton-Cincinnati) once route density works.
why_now: Reshoring is adding machined and fabricated volume in the US while environmental permits have made new plating, anodize and coating lines almost impossible to build. Existing finishers are running full but inefficiently. Lightweight route and tote software plus cheap dispatch tools remove the reason this stayed a hand-arranged, phone-call business.
revenue_model: $55-$95 per stop or tote pickup, an 8-12% margin on capacity-slot resale, and a $299/month booking and tracking subscription. Roughly 40 active shops on one corridor gets to $1M ARR. Later, purchase or co-develop a permitted finishing line inside a 'factory condo'.
non_obvious_insight: An anodize or zinc cycle takes hours. Most of the lead time is a batch waiting for a truck and waiting for enough peers to fill a rack. That is a logistics-and-pooling problem hiding inside what everyone treats as a process-capacity problem, and it is solvable without building a single tank.
first_30_days: Lease one box truck or contract a local courier per stop. Interview 15 shops and 4 finishers. Launch one route on Tuesdays and Thursdays with 8 pilot shops at $65 per stop. Get two finishers to guarantee 48-hour processing for pooled lots in exchange for weekly committed volume. Track everything in Airtable with printed QR tags and text updates, and publish on-time-in-full data after 6 weeks.

title: Robot Basecoating for Tabletop Miniature Armies
one_liner: A batch service where vision-guided robot airbrush cells prime, zenithal-shade and basecoat plastic miniatures so hobbyists only paint the details.
customer: Tabletop wargamers with unpainted backlogs, tournament players who need painted armies, and commission-painter studios who subcontract the tedious stages.
problem: An army is 100+ models, and priming and basecoating are the tedious first 60% of the work. Commission painters charge $10-60 per model and take months. Games Workshop's FY2026 revenue of GBP 626.8M shows the scale of the hobby.
solution: Customers ship assembled models. A low-cost robot arm learned from expert airbrushers primes, zenithal-shades and single-color basecoats. Humans QA and finish edges, and the army returns in about 10 days. Start human-in-the-loop with teleoperation and automate progressively.
why_now: Low-cost open-source robot arms and imitation-learning policies matured in 2025. A search for a commercial robot-airbrush painting service for miniatures found none.
revenue_model: $1.50-4 per model, $99-399 per army, and a subscription 'paint club' for batches.
non_obvious_insight: The community fetishizes painting but dislikes the first stage. The robot needs consistency, not artistry, on surfaces that hidden under detail work. Human painters keep the premium layer and become customers and distribution.
first_30_days: Hand-airbrush 50 armies to validate price and turnaround through r/Warhammer and local clubs. Build a teleop rig with a ~$3k arm and airbrush. Ship the first 20 orders.

title: Liquid-Cooling Leak-Test Crews for AI Data Centers
one_liner: A specialty crew of journeyman plumbers that flushes, fills, pressure-tests and photo-documents every quick-disconnect in AI liquid-cooled halls, sold per rack to neoclouds and the contractors building for them.
customer: Neocloud and colocation operators building liquid-cooled GPU halls, and the mechanical and general contractors on those builds who carry the commissioning schedule and the liability.
problem: Liquid cooling for AI racks turns data centers into plumbing systems with hundreds of quick-disconnect pairs per rack and coolant loops feeding hardware worth millions. Leaks at quick disconnects were among the failures during the first field ramps of dense racks. Commissioning delays on a large hall cost on the order of $14M per month, and pipefitters and mechanical trades are named in July 2026 surveys as one of the top three labor gaps. Much of the rack-level wet work is done by data-center technicians and electricians who were never trained in flushing, air removal, test discipline or cleanliness, so tests pass on Friday and a fitting drips on Monday.
solution: A three-person 'wet-work pod' (two journeymen and one apprentice) with a kit: pressure-decay test rig at 1.5x operating pressure, a filtered flush cart with a particle counter, a glycol refractometer, a borescope, UV dye and torque tools. The pod flushes and fills loops, purges air, tests and re-tests, and logs every quick-disconnect with a photo, QR tag and rack serial, generating the traceable leak-test record the lender, the insurer and the operator want. Priced per rack or per pod-day, with a commissioning-window guarantee. Later add a warranty-backed re-inspection after thermal cycling.
why_now: Liquid cooling roughly doubled in 2025 and is forecast to keep compounding, the racks in the field have far higher density and leak sensitivity than air-cooled halls, and the labor gap in pipefitting is the acknowledged constraint. Operators are paying premiums for anyone with liquid-loop experience, and the cost of one leaked rack dwarfs the cost of the crew.
revenue_model: $350-900 per rack for flush, fill, test and documented verification, or $2,400-3,500 per pod-day with a minimum engagement, plus paid re-inspection visits and a documentation package fee. Gross margin of 30-40% after paying journeymen $75-95 per hour, well above residential wages.
non_obvious_insight: Data center people think the hard part is the chip; plumbers know the hard part is water. Air pockets, thermal expansion, dirty new pipe (flux, cutting oil, thread dope), dissimilar metals and untested O-rings are what leak, and a documented test is worth more than a passed one. For a plumbing shop this is also a retention weapon: a road crew at data center rates keeps a 35-year-old journeyman from leaving the trade.
first_30_days: Use permit filings to find three data center builds within driving distance and call the mechanical superintendents. Offer a paid two-day leak-test audit on one row of racks. In parallel finish subcontractor prequalification (OSHA 30, insurance, NDA, background checks) and build the QR-tag and photo log. Put two journeymen from the shop on a rotating schedule so the residential business does not suffer.

title: Wearable-Verified PE Credit for ESA Families
one_liner: Turn any kid's fitness tracker into an audit-proof PE transcript line and an ESA service receipt.
customer: Homeschool and microschool families, co-ops and umbrella schools (about $10-15 per student per month). ESA administrators and clearinghouses (compliance contracts). Gyms and studios that want to bill ESA funds.
problem: PE is the least-supported homeschool subject. ESA homeschoolers get a fraction of what private-school kids do (about $2,000 versus $10,474 in Texas) and must spend in a closed vendor marketplace. ESA programs are audit-anxious. Local climbing gyms, swim schools and martial-arts studios cannot clear vendor onboarding. Screen-fatigued parents want real movement documented.
solution: An app plus a $40-60 band, or existing Garmin/Apple/Polar data shared with parent consent. It logs moderate-to-vigorous minutes and coach-attested skill milestones. It converts them into Carnegie-unit PE credit on a transcript issued through a partner accredited umbrella school. It also generates tamper-evident 'service delivered' receipts for ESA reimbursement. A vendor-of-record wrapper handles W-9, insurance and background-check attestations so a local gym can bill ESA funds. Parents control the data and only summaries leave the family account.
why_now: With 31 states opted into the 2027 federal scholarship credit and ESAs expanding, auditors and SGOs will demand evidence that services were actually delivered. Homeschool ESA marketplaces are closed and clunky. Alpha School has normalized heart-rate monitoring of kids, consumer wearables are ubiquitous, and 61% of teachers want less screen time.
revenue_model: $12 per student per month from families or co-ops. $2-5 per verified session or receipt from ESA clearinghouses. A 5-8% vendor-of-record fee on gym and studio ESA billings.
non_obvious_insight: As tens of billions of public scholarship dollars start to flow, the winning tools will be the ones that produce evidence of delivered service as a byproduct. A heart-rate trace is a hard-to-fake delivery receipt, and PE is the one subject where wearables give clean proof. Fitness providers' idle daytime hours are the supply, and education compliance is the demand.
first_30_days: In one ESA state (AZ or FL), recruit 8-10 homeschool co-ops and 3-5 climbing, martial-arts or swim studios. Sign an accredited umbrella school to issue the PE credit. Enroll about 100 kids for a semester at $12 a month. Ship a minimal web app that ingests Garmin/Apple Health exports plus coach attestation. Take the pilot data to one ESA clearinghouse.

title: Vendor-Neutral ELD Log Auditor and DataQs Filer
one_liner: An independent audit that catches the log errors ELD vendors create, and files the FMCSA challenge when they become violations.
customer: Owner-operators and carriers with 1-50 trucks, plus small DOT-compliance consultants who would white-label it. The driver or carrier owner pays.
problem: ELD software errors turn into violations and fines, and vendor support does not fix them. BigRoad reviewers say 'BigRoad could equal BigFines' because it will 'change your duty status randomly on its own'. They also report that it 'automatically switches to driving', that split sleeper 'doesn't work at all', and that a recent update left them unable to sign their logs. A Motive reviewer says 'it tells me I'm two hours into violation yet in the six past days I've driven 41 hours', and another says 'they cannot take off the violations from ELD'. Motive's following-distance alerts also draw complaints: it 'dings you for following too close when cars pass you in the next lane'.
solution: The driver or carrier emails the standard ELD output file, which every FMCSA-registered ELD must be able to produce (49 CFR 395, Appendix A). The system works with any ELD vendor. It rebuilds the duty timeline and flags implausible auto-driving events, unassigned driving, edits without annotations, split-sleeper and personal-conveyance miscalculations, and form-and-manner errors. It sends a weekly 'audit-ready' report before roadside inspections or compliance audits. When a violation is cited, it assembles a DataQs challenge packet (FMCSA's data-correction request) with the log evidence, GPS or fuel-card timestamps and vendor error messages, ready for the carrier to file.
why_now: FMCSA's DataQs site says that as of September 18, 2026 the revised requirements for State data reviews are in effect, with the stated aim that 'drivers receive their proper due process'. That change is 10 days old and makes challenging bad violations a more credible use of a carrier's time. ELD vendors are still shipping regressions (BigRoad reviewers describe updates that broke log signing and split sleeper in 2026), so the error volume keeps producing challenge-worthy events.
revenue_model: $9 per truck per month for the weekly audit. $99-$199 per DataQs packet. A white-label plan for DOT consultants at $500/month for up to 100 trucks. Later: a discount referral to an insurer that rewards clean, audited logs.
non_obvious_insight: Drivers cannot tell whether the ELD or the driver is wrong, and the vendor has no incentive to tell them. The federal ELD standard gives an open data pipe, so a third party can check any vendor's logs without a vendor integration, and the answer is more credible because the auditor does not sell ELDs. Evidence: BigRoad ELD app reviews (duty status flips, split sleeper broken, 'BigFines') at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=674704833/sortby=mostrecent/xml. Motive reviews (false violation time, violations the vendor cannot remove, following-distance algorithm complaints) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/gomotive.com. The DataQs process and the Sept 18, 2026 change are on FMCSA's own page at https://dataqs.fmcsa.dot.gov/. Carriers already pay for DataQs help, so the willingness to pay is proven. The new part is vendor-neutral log analysis with a challenge packet ready to file.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: read the ELD output file spec, build a parser using FMCSA's sample files and one test ELD, and write the 8 error checks. Days 10-20: recruit 10 owner-operators from trucker Facebook groups and forums for a free audit of their last 8 days. Days 20-30: show each one the specific errors found, charge for the first DataQs packets, and sign 2-3 DOT consultants for the white-label plan. Get a compliance professional to review the packet format.

title: RoboManual: Appliance Manuals Written for Humanoids
one_liner: A licensed library of articulated digital twins and operating procedures (where to press, how the latch moves, how much force) for the 500 most common home appliances, sold to home-robot makers and to appliance brands that want their products to be robot-ready.
customer: Home and general-purpose robot companies and robot foundation-model labs (1X, Figure, Sunday-type startups, Tesla-adjacent teams, lab groups training manipulation policies). Later, appliance OEMs (dishwashers, washers, ovens, fridges) and retailers.
problem: Home humanoids ship into thousands of models of dishwashers, washers, ovens and jars. 1X's Neo, the first humanoid actually delivered to consumers, leans on remote human operators for tasks like laundry and dishes because robots do not know how to operate your specific machine. Appliance makers wrote manuals for humans; nobody owns the equivalent for machines: hinge axes, latch travel, button actuation force, timing and failure modes.
solution: A physical-measurement studio that scans and instruments appliances. It produces articulated 3D assets (URDF/USD) with annotated affordances (press points, required force, latch and door kinematics, common jams) plus step-by-step procedure graphs and video of human demonstrations. Delivered as a dataset license and a lookup API keyed by model number, so a robot can scan a label and retrieve its operating plan. Every deployed robot's failures feed back to update the manual. Appliance OEMs pay for inclusion and a 'robot-graspable' certification.
why_now: Consumer humanoids started shipping in 2026 (1X Neo, $20k or $499/month) and are teleop-assisted, so every learned procedure has a direct dollar value in removed operator hours. Sim-based training pipelines are hungry for articulated real-world assets. Industrial pilots by Figure, Agility and Apptronik make robot makers seek reusable object knowledge.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses of $25-100k per year per lab or robot maker, per-lookup API fees at scale, OEM inclusion and certification fees ($20-50k per product line), and custom scan projects.
non_obvious_insight: Robots do not lack general knowledge about 'a dishwasher'. They lack knowledge about this latch and this button lag. The moat is physical measurement labor plus fleet feedback, not AI, so big labs will not bother to build it early. It is the 'second manual' of the appliance industry.
first_30_days: Partner with a scratch-and-dent appliance outlet and a repair shop for scan access. Capture 50-100 top-selling dishwashers, washers, dryers, microwaves and ovens with photogrammetry, a force gauge and video of human operation. Produce cleaned articulated assets with affordance labels and sell a pilot pack to 2-3 home-robot startups at $25-50k.

title: Succession Roll-Up for Retiring Solo Therapists
one_liner: A service that brokers and buys retiring solo practices and transitions clients to vetted associates, so clients are not orphaned and young clinicians inherit a full caseload.
customer: Retiring psychologists, social workers and family therapists (paid through fees and earn-outs) and early-career clinicians or group practices paying a transition fee, roughly $3-10k per practice.
problem: A large share of independent therapists are past 55, and solo practitioners typically just close, leaving clients scrambling. New clinicians spend 12-24 months building a caseload. Consolidation is capturing platform-dependent supply (Spring Health acquiring Alma, Jan 2026; Universal Health Services buying Talkspace for $835M, Mar 2026), but nobody owns practice transition the way dental service organizations do.
solution: A 6-12 month warm-handoff program consistent with ethics codes and client choice: records custody, client consent workflow, payer-panel reassignment through a group NPI, referral-source handover, and an earn-out to the retiring clinician funded by the successor's collections. Software handles consent, records and payer onboarding. Later: an MSO owning the transitioned practices.
why_now: Back-office rails built by Alma and Grow (Grow raised $150M) now make onboarding an associate cheap. Boomer therapists retire through 2025-30, and platform consolidation leaves the independent tail unowned.
revenue_model: Transition fee (5-10% of annual practice revenue), earn-out spread, later MSO margin, and buyer-side subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is consolidating the platform, but nobody is consolidating the goodwill of retiring clinicians, which is the cheapest source of established caseloads and referral relationships and the one asset that walks out the door every Friday.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 retiring clinicians through state association mailings and Psychology Today profiles. Match five with early-career clinicians. Have a healthcare attorney draft an ethics-reviewed transition agreement, and complete two transitions at a flat $3k each.

title: Seasonal Staff Housing from Banned Rentals
one_liner: Master-lease flats stranded by short-term-rental bans and sublet them by the bed, with employer-guaranteed rent, to short-staffed hotels in the same destination.
customer: Hotels, resorts and restaurant groups with 50-400 seasonal staff in Palma, Ibiza, Barcelona coast and similar hotspots (start in the Balearics). Secondary customer: small owners whose licences are ending.
problem: Insiders frame STR bans as residents versus tourists, with owners as the losers. The overlooked fact is that banned owners have empty flats and fear 12-month tenancy law, while the hotel next door cannot hire because staff cannot find housing. Nobody sits in the middle to handle leases, furnishing, inspections and deposits.
solution: An asset-light intermediary signs 6-11 month leases with owners under a structure vetted by local counsel. The hotel guarantees the rent and places its own staff. We handle furnishing, house rules, inspections and optional payroll-deduction of rent, and charge per bed. The wedge is one Palma pilot with 3 hotels and about 30 flats.
why_now: Palma has a full ban, Barcelona bans all STRs in Nov 2028 after Spain's top court upheld it in Oct 2025, and Madrid restricts listings. Spain fined Airbnb $75M in Dec 2025, so the stranded supply is real. Spain still had about 97M visitors, so hotels are staffing to record demand.
revenue_model: A 12-18% management fee on rent, or a EUR 40-70 per bed per month spread, plus a placement fee from the hotel and a fee for guaranteeing rent to the owner.
non_obvious_insight: A ban strands supply as well as demand, and the best tenant for that supply is the employer of the people who service tourism. Employer-guaranteed rent is better credit than any nomad or mid-term tenant, which lets owners accept lower rents for zero vacancy risk.
first_30_days: Contact HR and operations heads at 15 hotels through the Mallorca hoteliers' federation and LinkedIn, and sign 3 letters of intent for 10-20 beds each. Recruit 30 owners through ex-STR property managers and owner groups. Pay a local lawyer EUR 3-5K for a lease template. Sign leases only after the hotel LOIs are in.
